# How to Use a Rowing Machine: Proper Form in 4 Steps (Plus the 5 Mistakes Almost Every Beginner Makes)


Last updated November 2026


Two minutes of setup before your first stroke saves you a sore back later.


**Short answer:** To use a rowing machine, strap your feet in across the widest part of your foot, set a low resistance, and repeat one sequence. Push with your legs, lean back slightly, then pull the handle to your lower ribs. Come back in reverse: arms out, body forward, knees bend. Legs, body, arms as you push away. Arms, body, legs as you come back. Push quickly, return slowly.


That's the whole stroke. The tricky part is keeping that order for 20 minutes while your arms keep trying to cut in line, and that's where most beginners need help, whether it comes from a coach, a video of themselves or the screen on an Aviron Strong Series.

## How Do You Set Up a Rowing Machine Before Your First Stroke?


Check five things before you pull the handle:


- **Feet.** Tighten the strap across the widest part of your foot, just behind your toes. If it sits too far back, you lose the solid platform your legs push against. Your heels can lift a little as you slide forward. That's normal.
- **Foot width.** Most rowers only adjust for shoe size. The Strong Series footplates also slide wider or narrower, so you can row at your own hip width instead of the machine's.
- **Resistance.** Start low. Numbers are below.
- **Grip.** Fingers over the handle, thumbs underneath, wrists flat. Hold it loosely enough that your forearms aren't burning before your legs are. The Strong Series handlebar is 19 inches wide and rotates, so your wrists can stay neutral.
- **Screen.** Put stroke rate (SPM) and time where you can see them. That's all you need in week one.


The footplates adjust for width as well as shoe size, so everyone in the house can row at their own stance.


## What Are the 4 Steps of the Rowing Stroke?


Every stroke runs through the same four positions in the same order. Coaches call the push the drive and the trip back the recovery. To judge your lean, picture a clock face beside you with 12 o'clock straight up. That cue comes from rowing coach Katie Wason in[Consumer Reports' rowing guide](https://www.consumerreports.org/health/rowing-machines/how-to-use-a-rowing-machine-to-get-a-great-workout-a1084933380/) .


### Step 1: The Catch


Slide forward until your shins are vertical, or as close as feels comfortable. Arms straight, shoulders relaxed, back long, and your body tipped slightly forward from the hips to about 1 o'clock. You should feel coiled and ready to push, with your chest up.


### Step 2: The Drive


Push through your feet with your arms still straight. As your legs pass about halfway, your body starts swinging back from the hips. Your arms only pull once your legs are nearly flat. Legs, body, arms. Your legs make most of the power, so if your arms go first, you're leaving your biggest muscles out of it.


### Step 3: The Finish


Legs extended but not locked, body leaning back a little to about 11 o'clock, and the handle at your lower ribs with your elbows just past your sides and your wrists flat. Don't lie back like you're in a deck chair. A small lean, braced through your core, is plenty.


### Step 4: The Recovery


Now reverse it. Your arms straighten until the handle passes your knees, your body tips forward to 1 o'clock, and only then do your knees bend to slide you back to the catch. Arms, body, legs. Take your time on this part. Wason suggests coming forward at about half the speed of your drive, which also gives you a moment to breathe.


**1. The catch.** Shins vertical, arms straight, leaning to about 1 o'clock. **2. The drive.** Legs push first. The arms are still straight. **3. The finish.** Legs long, a slight lean back, handle at the lower ribs. **4. The recovery.** Arms go out first. The knees wait.


One stroke on the Strong Series, in four frames.


## What Resistance and Stroke Rate Should a Beginner Use?


Lower than you think, on both counts.


**Resistance.** Concept2, which makes the rowers in most gyms,[recommends starting its damper at 3 to 5](https://www.concept2.com/training/articles/damper-setting) out of 10 and warns that setting it too high "can exhaust your muscles before you reap the full cardiovascular benefit rowing provides." More resistance feels like more work, but how hard you push is what sets the intensity.


On the Strong Series, resistance runs in 16 steps from 10 to 160. Aviron's guidance is 10 to 100 for cardio and 110 to 160 for strength, so start near the bottom of the cardio range. Then test it with 20 strokes. If your back rounds or your arms jump in early, drop a level. If the handle feels like it's attached to nothing, go up one.


**Stroke rate.** SPM (strokes per minute) counts how many strokes you take each minute. New rowers almost always go too fast, because a high rate feels busy. Put the effort into each push instead and keep the rate down. These ranges come from Concept2's guidance, via Consumer Reports:


Effort Stroke rate How it feels


Easy rows and technique practice 16 to 24 spm You could hold a conversation


Most workouts 24 to 30 spm Short sentences only


Sprints Over 30 spm Talking is off the table


For your first couple of weeks, stay in the low 20s. If your stroke rate creeps past 30 on an easy row, you're probably rushing the recovery.

## What Are the 5 Most Common Rowing Machine Mistakes?


Most beginners make at least one of these, and most of them come from breaking the order: legs, body, arms, then arms, body, legs.


Mistake How you'll know The fix


1. Pulling with your arms first Your arms and shoulders tire before your legs do Keep your elbows straight until your legs are nearly flat


2. Lunging or rounding at the catch Your lower back aches after a session Lean only to 1 o'clock, keep your chest up, and drop a resistance level


3. Bending your knees too early Your hands have to go up and over your knees on the way forward Arms out, body forward, then knees


4. Rushing the slide The seat races forward and your stroke rate creeps past 30 Count "one" on the push and "two, three" on the way forward


5. Maxing out the resistance Your legs are cooked in five minutes and your form falls apart Start low in the cardio range and go up one level at a time


[Concept2 describes mistake 3](https://www.concept2.com/training/improve-your-rowing-technique) as "rowing over a barrel," which is exactly how it feels. The quickest way to spot any of them is to prop your phone on a chair and film 30 seconds from the side, as Wason suggests. Or let the screen do the watching.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Are you supposed to lean back on a rowing machine?


A little. At the finish, lean back to about 11 o'clock with your core braced. Concept2 calls an extreme layback "a weak position" because leaning further doesn't add useful length to your stroke.


### Should your heels lift on a rowing machine?


A little, at the catch, is fine.[Concept2's technique guide](https://www.concept2.com/training/rowing-technique) says your heels "may lift as needed." Keep the strap across the widest part of your foot so your feet stay connected through the whole stroke.


### How long should a beginner row?


Start with 10 to 15 minutes, three times a week, and build toward 20 to 30 minutes over your first month. Short sessions with clean form beat long ones where the order falls apart at the end. More in[how long you should use a rowing machine](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/how-long-use-rowing-machine/) .


### Is 20 minutes of rowing a day enough?


For general health, yes. The[WHO recommends](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7719906/) 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity a week. Twenty minutes of moderate rowing on most days gets you close, and four hard 20-minute sessions cover the vigorous target.


### Why does my lower back hurt after rowing?


Usually it's form: rounding forward at the catch, leaning too far back at the finish, or heaving with your back before your legs have pushed. Drop a resistance level, slow your stroke rate and film yourself from the side. If the pain sticks around, see a doctor or physical therapist. Our guide to[preventing rowing machine injuries](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/rowing-machine-injuries/) has more.
